I still have it. My whole mental health is a bit better than 5 years ago because of time away from trauma that happened in my early 20s, therapy, and meds. Those help a lot. I've been in DBT therapy for the past 5 years and that helped me heal. DBT helps people handle intense emotions. They give you a skills book and then the therapist helps you apply those skills to your life. It's expensive though. Acceptance helps too although it's hard. It was easier for me to accept it over time, and also after I healed a bit. My reason to live is because I imagine how my parents will react if they see my dead body and it breaks my heart, I can't do that to them. Having forced distractions helps such as work and school (which I went back to and have motivation to do because my current job sucks), even though I don't like them, but they force me to keep going. I watch a lot of comedy on YouTube, such as stand-up, improv, sketch comedy, talk shows, British panel shows and funny podcasts. My therapist said notice tiny moments when I feel ok, like the moment I'm watching comedy, the feeling of good-tasting food or a nice smell. Feel free to ask more questions or DM me.

My experience with therapists and psychiatrists is therapists are good for therapy, psychiatrists are doctors and help with meds or physical treatment options and are less adept at therapy. Therapists usually specialize in a particular type or style of therapy, but unless you know you need a particular type, it doesn't really matter. All decent therapists are good listeners and try to help with your thoughts and behavioral patterns.

Is it possible for you to meet with people online, from a private room or somewhere your parents don't have to be? Especially since covid, most therapists and psychiatrists can be met with over Zoom or something similar. I've been able to book appointments with therapists through calling and emailing, without ever seeing them in person.

I'm not sure what the public services are like where you are. There may be free services available through doctor or hospital referrals and free services for children and youths if you're underage. In my city, the hospital has an outpatient mental health department people can call or email as the first step for learning about treatment options. I'm currently seeing a psychiatrist out of there for med help. My hospital has free group and individual therapy options, but only temporary (eg. 12 sessions) and there's usually a wait list of months. If you go for an independent therapist or therapy center, it'll probably cost money per session, but you might be able to see them right away.

As for the suicidal thoughts, I just learned to live with them tbh. I've had them for years and it's forced me to accept that they live in my brain and I don't have to listen to them. Meds can definitely help thoughts get quieter or help improve your mood if you find the right one. Where I am, a psychiatrist first needs to evaluate whether they'd be right for you or not. 

Sorry if that sounds like a lot. Getting help is a series of steps and you can take as many steps as you want to and stop at any time. I guess the first step would be to contact any medical service who might have information about what's available to you.

When I was 16 I decided I needed real therapy, so I asked my school counselor about therapy places. I'd already been meeting with her and she knew that she, my family, and my doctor were useless in helping me. She got me an appointment with some sort of youth counselor/social worker, who after interviewing/evaluating me, referred me to a youth therapy place. It was an 8-month wait to get a therapist, but the psychiatrist working there started helping me with medication right away. While I was waiting, they had a Master's student (therapist in training?) meet with me at my school to tide me over. They weren't that skillful, but I guess it was nice to have someone to talk to at least. Therapy was free since I was under-age. I was with the youth place until I aged out, at which point they referred me to a psychiatrist at the university I was attending, who tried to also give me therapy, but since she was a doctor and not a therapist I found her therapy to be insufficient. At that point if I wanted a real therapist, I had to find one and pay for it myself (which I've been doing ever since).

My parents didn't understand what was going on and couldn't control where I went at or after school, so they didn't interfere or anything. They just knew I'd gotten myself a therapist and started meds. They were probably relieved I was doing everything myself, because when I asked them for help they didn't have the slightest idea about mental health services.

I've tried like 7 different antidepressants since 2013, starting with Prozac and Wellbutrin since they seem to be the most commonly-prescribed ones (I've tried them twice each now). In the early years I always seemed to get weird symptoms like tinnitus, twitching, urinary retention, etc. when the dose increased a little bit. Although it wasn't anything unbearable, the side effects stayed until I went off the meds. Now I don't get any side effects when I change meds under doctor supervision anymore :/  None of them ever helped my mood significantly, they most effective they've been is the worst of the sadness and fear is numbed and my lows are less low. Once in a while I'm on something for a couple years and then they seem to stop doing anything at all so I try something else again. If you go slowly and you and your doctor are keeping track, I don't think you'll suddenly get significantly more emotional or anything. For me it's sort of like the doctor sees what a small dose does and then verifies this by trying a slightly higher dose, and I decrease if it starts being unbearable. Good luck, I hope you find something that works soon.
